A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VRoPE and contain readable text, equations, figures and tables that support reliable comparison. v1 ends after its references; v2 adds Appendices A-E, including relocated discussion and new material.

before.justification: v1 reports original video benchmark evaluations, long-video retrieval experiments, attention visualizations and component ablations in Section 5 and Tables 1-4.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds boundary-attention measurements, EventBench evaluations, robustness analyses and experiments with another backbone and training configuration.

M1.justification: The four spatial directions, frame offsets and text encoding are retained under renamed components. However, v1 Eqs. 6-8 and v2 Eqs. 6-9 exchange the directions assigned to channels j=4k+1 and j=4k+2. Since RoPE frequencies depend on j, this is a small change in the written encoding beyond relabeling; the PDFs do not establish an implementation change or rerun.

E1.justification: v2 adds EventBench's event-centered temporal evaluation and OpenVid-1M video-text training data in Appendix B, extending coverage within the existing video-language domain. Section 5.1 also stops listing OneVision in the Qwen2 fine-tuning mixture, although the PDFs do not establish whether this corrects the description or reflects changed training.

E2.justification: The matched comparisons retain RoPE and RoPE-3D, with RoPE-2D, RoPE-Share and RoPE-Compact retained in the variant ablation. New evaluations reuse RoPE and RoPE-3D. Appendix D expands descriptions of existing comparators without establishing changed procedures.

E3.justification: Appendix B.4 introduces a separate SigLIP-2/Qwen3-8B configuration using 32 frames, 384×384 resolution and approximately 1 million pre-training and 3 million instruction-tuning samples. v2 also adds eight-frame evaluation and a boundary-attention measurement procedure. These substantially extend the experimental settings beyond the retained 16-frame, 224×224 main evaluation.

E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative video-text boundary attention analysis (Table 1), performance stratified by video duration (Table 7), sparse-frame robustness testing (Table 8), and a query-specific attention and prediction case study (Figure 5). These examine continuity, duration sensitivity and event localization beyond v1's retained aggregate heatmaps and component ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its experiments. The additional averages and performance differences in v2 do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The accuracy values in v1 Tables 1-4 are retained in v2 Tables 2-5. v2 adds boundary-attention, EventBench, duration-specific, eight-frame and Qwen3-8B results, plus a qualitative prediction example. Within the new settings, VRoPE versus RoPE scores are 40.9 versus 38.9 on eight-frame Video-MME and 62.40 versus 61.92 average with Qwen3-8B; these are newly reported comparisons rather than v1-to-v2 performance gains.

T1.justification: The formal encoding definition changes the coordinate-to-channel ordering, with the corresponding one-dimensional specialization changing from (w,-w,w,-w) to (w,w,-w,-w). Otherwise, v2's explicit temporal-offset equation restates v1's H+W-1 frame update. The RoPE preliminaries remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that VRoPE preserves spatiotemporal structure, reduces positional attention bias and enables smooth video-text transitions, improving video understanding and retrieval across backbones. Component renaming and broader experimental support do not materially alter these central contributions; the conclusion is retained.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the implicit-temporal explanation with frame-center alignment reasoning and connects boundary attention, existing retrieval deficits and the new case study to discontinuity and localization errors. Appendix B adds interpretations concerning sparse-frame robustness and applicability across training configurations. The model-size limitation now includes 8B, while limitations concerning other modalities remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B.4 supplies the added training recipe's resolutions, frame counts and sampling quantities; Appendix D provides explicit positional-ID descriptions for RoPE-Share and RoPE-Compact. Appendix E adds a research-only model licensing statement. Existing optimizer and hardware details remain, and both abstracts still describe code as forthcoming.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Qwen2.5-VL, EventBench, OpenVid-1M, SigLIP-2 and Qwen3, while removing the Vicuna, Qwen2 and standalone Su multimodal-position reflection references. The related-work argument remains centered on limitations of existing RoPE adaptations, so research positioning changes only modestly.

P1.justification: Section 4 is substantially rewritten and reorganized: Symmetric Bias Mitigation comes first, and Cross-Modal Continuity Rotation becomes Temporal Centered Arrangement with a different explanatory narrative. The dimensional-adaptability discussion moves from Section 4.3 to Appendix A, and Appendices B-E organize additional results, explanations and licensing. Abstract, introduction and author information also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, and v1's separate architecture and method illustrations become the combined, redesigned Figure 3 in v2. v2 adds five tables and a qualitative attention figure, and rearranges existing tables. The RoPE-2D continuity marker is corrected. The original aggregate-attention and retrieval heatmaps are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens an already substantial evaluation through direct boundary-attention measurements, event and sparse-frame tests, and another backbone/data configuration. Rewritten method explanations, redesigned diagrams and the corrected RoPE-2D marker improve clarity. These provide a limited net quality gain, while unexplained changes to the Qwen2 training description and encoding assignments leave reproducibility ambiguities, and uncertainty reporting remains absent.
